opus-5.5.text:
I think the difference is mostly about emphasis and timescale. Many companies, especially the big labs, are betting heavily on scaling: more data, more compute, bigger models, and then a lot of engineering to make that pipeline efficient. That's a very reasonable bet. Scaling has worked remarkably well, and as a company you need things that pay off on a predictable schedule.

My interest is slightly different. When I say "AI for AI," I mean using AI, and ideas borrowed from science, to understand AI itself. Can we treat a neural network like a physical system? Can we find its "laws," its "phase transitions," its conserved quantities? Can we design architectures that are more interpretable from the start, so that when a model learns something we can read it out instead of just observing that the loss went down? That's partly why I worked on things like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks and on mechanistic questions like grokking. The goal isn't to beat a frontier model on a benchmark. It's to make the science of these systems less like alchemy.

So I see it as complementary rather than competitive. Industry is pushing the frontier of capability, and someone needs to build the theory and the tools that explain why that frontier looks the way it does. Historically, the steam engine came before thermodynamics, but thermodynamics is what let people build much better engines. I'd like my work to play a small role like that.

There's also a practical side. Academic researchers can't compete on compute, so we have to compete on ideas. That pushes you toward questions that are more fundamental, like efficiency, interpretability, and inductive biases, that a scaling-first strategy might overlook. I'm not saying scaling is wrong. I just think that if we only scale, we may reach very capable systems that we don't really understand, and to me that's both scientifically unsatisfying and a bit risky. Understanding is the part I care about most.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that what we're trying to do is pretty different in spirit from what most companies mean when they say "AI for AI," even though on the surface the words sound the same.

Most of the industry version of this is about using AI to accelerate the engineering loop: writing code faster, running more experiments, automating hyperparameter search, maybe having models help design the next generation of models. That's enormously valuable, and I don't want to dismiss it. If you're OpenAI or Google or Anthropic, you have a very clear objective function, which is essentially: make the next model better, cheaper, faster, and keep the flywheel going. Everything is oriented toward scaling the existing recipe more efficiently.

What I care about is something more like AI for the science of AI. We still don't really understand why these systems work. We have a lot of empirical phenomena, scaling laws, grokking, emergence, in-context learning, and we have very few first-principles explanations for them. My background is in physics, and in physics you'd never be satisfied with "it works, we don't know why, let's build a bigger one." You'd want the equations. So the question I'm interested in is: can we use AI itself as a tool to help us discover those principles? Can AI help us find the right abstractions, the right mathematical objects, the right experiments that reveal mechanism rather than just performance?

That's why I've spent so much time on things like interpretability and on architectures like KANs, where the goal isn't necessarily to beat a transformer on a benchmark. The goal is to build systems whose internal structure a human can actually read, so that the loop between the machine and the scientist stays open. If AI is going to do science, including the science of itself, I'd like humans to still be able to follow the argument.

So the relationship to industry is complementary, I'd say, not competitive. They're optimizing for capability under the current paradigm. I'm asking whether the current paradigm is the right one, and I'm hoping that if we understand it deeply enough, the next paradigm will look less like brute force and more like something we actually derived. I also think, frankly, that a lot of the safety questions and the efficiency questions end up being the same question once you look at them from the understanding side rather than the scaling side.

astra-6.text:
I think of AI-for-AI as asking how AI can help us understand and improve AI itself. There are different ways to pursue that. You can focus on automating parts of the research workflow, or you can use AI to help uncover principles that make the next round of research more effective.

For me, the scientific understanding is especially interesting. If an AI finds a better architecture or training method, can we also learn why it works? Can that result become an insight that applies beyond one experiment? That’s the kind of feedback loop I’d like to build: better AI helping us do better science, and better science helping us build better AI.

I wouldn’t draw a sharp boundary between that and what companies are doing. These approaches can be complementary. The distinction is more about what you prioritize: an immediate improvement in capability, or understanding that might enable many improvements later.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of AI for AI as asking whether AI can help us understand and improve AI itself. A lot of the work at companies is focused on making models more capable, and that’s valuable. The question I’m interested in is whether we can also make the process of discovery more systematic: can AI help us find new architectures, understand why they work, and turn those insights into better models?

Those goals can overlap. But I would distinguish getting a better result from gaining a better understanding. Ideally, we want a loop where better AI helps us do better research, and that research gives us both stronger AI and clearer principles.
